Crossway
KROSS-way
n. (a place where roads or paths cross or intersect; a junction offering escape in several directions)
A compound of cross, athwart, and way, a road or path.

Biblical Definition

Neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape; neither shouldest thou have delivered up those of his that did remain in the day of distress.

Obadiah's short prophecy is wholly devoted to Edom's sin against its brother nation Judah, and this verse names one of Edom's specific crimes: stationing men at the crossway, the junction points where fleeing Judean refugees might have escaped Jerusalem's destruction, in order to cut them off and hand them over to the invading enemy. The crossway, ordinarily a place of travel and connection, becomes in Edom's hands an ambush point exploited precisely because Edom was Judah's own kinsman, descended from Esau, Jacob's brother (Oba 1:10), making the betrayal a violation of covenant family loyalty, not merely ordinary wartime opportunism. Obadiah's judgment on Edom turns on this exact point: the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger (Oba 1:12) should have produced mourning and aid, not ambush at the crossway, and the prophecy's sweeping condemnation of Edom stands as Scripture's enduring warning against exploiting a kinsman's distress for gain.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Cross-way, noun, a road that crosses the main road; a point where ways intersect.

expand to see more

CROSS, a. Athwart; lying across another line or path.

WAY, n. A road, path, or route of travel.

CROSS-WAY, n. A junction or intersection of roads or paths.

Obadiah: Edom ambushed fleeing Judeans at the crossway.

Named as a violation of covenant kinship, not mere wartime opportunism.

Key Scripture

Oba 1:14 — "Neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape; neither shouldest thou have delivered up those of his that did remain in the day of distress."

Modern Corruption

Treating a kinsman's or neighbor's calamity as an opportunity for personal advantage, rather than an occasion for aid, is precisely the sin Obadiah names at the crossway and condemns without qualification.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation to exploit another's distress for gain, whether a nation's fall or an individual's misfortune, is as old as Edom and recurs in every age's opportunism.

The principle to recover is Obadiah's own indictment: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee (Oba 1:15). Standing at the crossway to profit from a brother's distress invites the same measure of judgment one dealt out, a sobering warning against every form of opportunistic betrayal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A plain English compound of cross, athwart or crossing, and way, a path or road — a crossway is simply a place where paths intersect, a point of decision and, in Obadiah, a point of betrayal.

"A violation of covenant family loyalty, not mere wartime opportunism."

"As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee — Obadiah's measured judgment."
